minutes.headline: Capital committee voted to keep its FY22 priority list, declining to add the primary school fire alarm replacement.
minutes.summary: The committee heard a late school department request to fund replacement of the obsolete primary school fire alarm system in the next fiscal year, using a state earmark. Members questioned why it had not been ranked higher earlier and whether anything new made it urgent. A motion to leave the prioritization unchanged was carried on a voice vote. A short discussion of the dollar threshold for capital projects was deferred until more members attend, and the next meeting was set for April 6.

budget_items.topic: State earmark and bond bill for primary school fire alarm
budget_items.what_was_said: An earmark in the state budget and a separate bond bill amount exist for the project, but the bond bill is considered unlikely to be released.
The project was earlier planned as a larger project for fiscal 23, then cut back to a smaller scope by leaving horns, strobes, door holders and the voice system in place.
The presenter said the large number of detectors is why the project is expensive, giving a per-detector price.

budget_items.topic: Spare parts cost for the existing system
budget_items.what_was_said: A member who is a purchasing agent said obsolete components for the old system can be found at a higher price than the presenter had suggested.
The town manager said the reserve fund via the finance committee would be the first source if the alarm failed, and it has not yet been drawn on this year.
The primary school air conditioning project was ranked very low among state-ranked projects, and design funding was approved in the prior year.
Members discussed raising the minimum cost for something to count as a capital project and pushing smaller items into the operating budget.

decisions.decision: The committee chose not to reprioritize its FY22 capital list to add the primary school fire alarm project; the school may seek it again next year or via another state earmark.
Discussion of fiscal policy and the capital threshold was postponed until more members are present.
The next meeting was set for April 6, with the policy discussion as the only agenda item.
The town manager will ask for a written determination on whether an earmark can be redirected to other uses.

what_happened.line: The Capital Planning Committee voted by voice to leave its FY22 priority list unchanged, so the primary school fire alarm replacement was not added.
The school department made a late request to fund replacing the obsolete primary school fire alarm next fiscal year, using a state earmark.
Members asked why the project had not ranked higher earlier and whether anything new made it urgent; the town manager named the reserve fund as the first source if the alarm failed.
The town manager will ask for a written determination on whether the earmark can be redirected to other uses.
Talk of raising the dollar threshold for capital projects was postponed until more members attend; the next meeting is April 6.

why_it_matters: The primary school's aging fire alarm system stays off the FY22 capital list, so any failure before it is funded would likely be paid from the reserve fund, which is set by the Finance Committee and is not a planned capital project.

A higher capital threshold would move smaller items out of the capital plan and into the operating budget, which could change what residents see on the capital list and in the yearly operating budget.
